_about: How a household gets its bank data into the sheet, by country. Rendered on the Setup tab and read by the bank-export skill. Paths change. Each entry says when it was documented (from product knowledge, by the agent that wrote this guide) and when, if ever, an agent verified it in a browser; the bank-export skill verifies before trusting a path and stamps 'verified'. Nothing here needs a password in a file.

countries.name: Australia
countries.best: The Consumer Data Right (open banking) is the regulated feed, but it reaches individuals only through accredited apps, not a personal API key. For a sheet-based household the reliable path is each bank's own CSV export, once a month, with Up's personal API as the exception that proves what the future looks like.
verdict: Works at every bank today, needs a person or a supervised agent, 10 to 20 minutes a month
A personal access token from the Up app gives JSON for your own accounts; no scraping, no password handling
Best in class, Up customers only
CDR through an accredited app (Frollo, PocketSmith, WeMoney)
Consented, continuous, every major bank; the app then exports CSV or syncs to a sheet
Good if you accept a third party
Hold your password, break on bank changes, against most banks' terms

institutions.name: Up
institutions.path: Up app → Settings → Data sharing → Export transactions (CSV by email), or create a Personal Access Token at api.up.com.au and pull JSON
institutions.columns: API: id, status, rawText, description, amount.value, settledAt, category; CSV: Time, BSB, Account, Transaction Type, Payee, Description, Category, Subcategory, Total, Currency, Fee, Round Up, Settled

institutions.name: American Express
institutions.path: amex.com.au → Statements & Activity → choose the period → Download (CSV or Excel)
institutions.columns: Date, Description, Card Member, Account #, Amount (positive = charge)
institutions.notes: Charges are positive and payments negative, the opposite of a bank account; the importer flips the sign. Statement periods do not match calendar months.

countries.agent: An agent may drive the browser to the export page while the person (or their password manager) signs in. The agent never types a password or a one-time code; it never reads them. It opens the bank, waits for the person to sign in, navigates to the export, chooses CSV and the dates, saves the file into sources/<account>/<yyyy-mm-dd>/ exactly as delivered, and signs out. Up is the exception: a read-only token in the keychain, no browser at all.

countries.name: New Zealand
countries.best: Akahu is the standout: an open-finance platform where an individual can create a personal app, connect their own accounts and pull transactions through an API, with the banks' blessing. Otherwise every bank exports CSV.
verdict: Your own API token over your own accounts, every major NZ bank

countries.name: United States
countries.best: There is no regulated personal feed yet (the CFPB's section 1033 rule is phasing in), so the practical path is either each bank's CSV download or a paid aggregator that lands rows straight in Google Sheets. Tiller Money does exactly that, which makes it the natural partner for a sheet-based household.
verdict: Tiller Money (Plaid feed into Google Sheets)
Transactions appear in your own sheet daily; you keep the sheet if you leave

Good apps, your data lives in theirs

landing.rule: A file is never edited. It is saved as delivered into sources/<account>/<download date>/, then an importer reads it, maps its columns to the Transactions tab (Txn ID, Date, Account ID, Bank description, Merchant, Amount, Category ID, Person, Receipt held, Note), de-duplicates against what the sheet already holds, categorises against the household's rules and history, and writes a review list for anything it is not sure of. Only after a person settles the review does it append rows. Nothing is ever appended twice because the Txn ID carries on from the last one in the sheet and the Compliance Checks tab fails on repeats.
map: Parsed in the bank's own format (dd/mm/yyyy in AU, mm/dd/yyyy in the US, ISO from APIs); stored as a date
One signed number: money in positive, money out negative. Debit/credit pairs and card-style positives are folded here
Exactly as delivered, so a row can always be found in the bank's own records
A cleaned name ("WOOLWORTHS 3021 BRUNSWICK" → Woolworths) from the household's rules; new ones are proposed, never guessed into history
From the Categories tab only; an unknown ID shows up in Compliance Checks
Jordan, Mia or Joint from the account or the card suffix
Left blank by the importer; a person adds them when it matters for tax
